clinicalPearls: The commonest of the inducible urticarias, in which stroking, scratching or rubbing the skin produces a linear itchy weal along the line of trauma
The term 'symptomatic' distinguishes the itchy, clinically significant form from simple dermographism, a common asymptomatic exaggeration of the normal triple response
Provocation by lightly stroking the skin, or by using a calibrated dermographometer, reproduces the weal and confirms the diagnosis
Weals develop within minutes and usually fade within about an hour, and itch may be prominent under tight clothing, after towelling or at night
It commonly affects young adults and is generally idiopathic, though it may be aggravated by heat, exercise or infection
The condition is benign but can significantly affect quality of life through persistent itch
Management centres on minimising skin friction and non-sedating antihistamines, with omalizumab an option for severe antihistamine-resistant disease
reference.pathophysiology: Symptomatic dermographism arises from an exaggerated response of cutaneous mast cells to mechanical shearing forces, such that minor stroking or rubbing triggers histamine and mediator release with a localised weal and flare along the line of trauma. The stimulus is thought to release or unmask an antigen that provokes IgE-dependent mast cell degranulation in susceptible skin. The result is a reproducible, mechanically induced urticaria that follows the exact pattern of the applied friction.
additionalDifferentials: Urticarial reaction to scabies or insect bites
Cutaneous mastocytosis with a positive Darier sign
additionalInvestigations: Provocation by stroking the skin or using a dermographometer to reproduce a linear weal
History correlating itch and weals with friction, clothing and towelling
Assessment for coexisting chronic spontaneous urticaria
Consideration of thyroid autoimmunity and other associations where chronic urticaria coexists
Examination for a Darier sign if mastocytosis is suspected
Basic screening for an aggravating infection where clinically relevant
redFlags: Persistent individual weals lasting more than a day or leaving bruising, suggesting urticarial vasculitis
Features suggesting mastocytosis, such as a strongly positive Darier sign
Severe refractory itch with major impact on sleep and daily life
reference.prognosis: Symptomatic dermographism is benign and often persists for several years before gradually resolving; most patients achieve good control with avoidance of friction and regular antihistamines, and the condition does not carry the systemic risks of some other physical urticarias.
pitfalls: Confusing symptomatic dermographism with simple asymptomatic dermographism and over-investigating the latter
Failing to reproduce the weal by provocation, leading to diagnostic uncertainty
Overlooking coexisting chronic spontaneous urticaria that also needs treatment
Not considering up-dosed antihistamines or omalizumab in disabling, resistant cases
references: British Association of Dermatologists guidance on chronic urticaria
management: Use a second-generation non-sedating H1 antihistamine as first-line therapy, with dose escalation if the response is inadequate
Advise avoidance of mechanical triggers such as friction, tight clothing, vigorous towelling and scratching, and use emollients
Consider adding an H2 antihistamine or a night-time sedating antihistamine for refractory itch
Use the anti-IgE agent omalizumab for antihistamine-refractory disease
Identify and treat aggravating factors such as heat and intercurrent infection, and assess for coexisting chronic spontaneous urticaria
Reassure about the benign course and eventual gradual resolution
